processing: A green tea made from a young bud and the two leaves below it, rolled into a small curved hook and fired.
harvest_season: Picked as young shoots of one bud and two leaves. Little is documented about a prized season for this grade in particular.
appearance_dry: Small, curled leaves bent like a fish hook, which is where the name comes from.
appearance_liquor: Typically clear yellow-green, as with other Thai Nguyen green teas.
appearance_wet: Small shoots open to show a bud with its two young leaves.
taste_profile: Follows the Tan Cuong pattern of a strong bitter touch on the tongue that turns into a deep, lingering sweetness.

brewing.notes: General guidance for Vietnamese green tea rather than a rule for this grade. Start short at about 80°C and lengthen only if the cup is thin.

vintage_note: Sold as a grade of Thai Nguyen green tea rather than by vintage. As is usual for green tea, the most recent harvest is the one to buy, and it should be drunk fresh. Ask the seller what picking standard the name means here.
description:
Móc câu means fish hook, and it describes both the shape of this Vietnamese green tea and its place in the Thai Nguyen grading ladder. It is one of the grades of Tan Cuong tea, with more leaf than the bud-focused dinh and tom non.

The picking rule is what defines it: one young bud plus the two leaves beneath it. Those leaves are rolled into a small curve and fired.

Expect the regional pattern of bitterness at the front of the tongue, followed by a sweetness that stays well after you swallow. More leaf generally means more body and grip than a pure bud grade, so hot water and long steeps are the usual mistakes.

The name alone guarantees little, so ask about the picking standard and where the tea was grown. If you enjoy it, compare it with a tom non from the same area to taste what the extra leaf does.
history:
Little is documented about when móc câu became a named grade. It is recorded as one of the grades of Tan Cuong tea, alongside dinh non and tom non, and the name comes from the hooked shape of the rolled leaf.

Its wider story is that of Thai Nguyen green tea, where grades are set by how much of the young shoot is picked.
